transcript:
Meeting header:
10:00 AM PDT — 2027-06-29 | Duration 45m
Attendees: Alex Morgan, Priya Patel, Samir Khan — Redwood; Liam O'Connor, Maria Chen, Thomas Reyes, Anya Patel — Rivermark

Summary: quick recap of last week's tuning, focused tests on TTFT and streaming, agreement to run an on-prem benchmark with longer sequence lengths and streaming enabled.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — we good?
[00:05] Liam: Yep, all here. Morning.
[00:07] Priya: Hi, thanks, we'll start with a short recap then jump into the perf numbers. Audio might be a little iffy on my side, sorry in advance.
[00:15] Alex: No worries. Recap: last week we saw decent throughput but TTFT was higher than expected when using the streaming path, particularly for 4k+ sequences. We ran kernel A vs kernel B on the hosted environment and saw ~18% difference in median and a larger impact on tail.
[00:32] Maria: Just to clarify, when you say kernel A, is that the APEX fused-attn variant or the one with the quantized matmul? I think last time the notes said "fused-attn v2" but the spreadsheet had a slightly different label so it's a bit confusing.
[00:45] Priya: Right, apologies — our exported labels were messy. Kernel A is the fused-attn path optimized for Ampere-style cards, Kernel B was the lower-memory quantized matmul path. The spreadsheet I'll send will have the explicit build IDs so you can match.
[01:02] Thomas: Cool. We're mainly trying to hit a 95th percentile around 220ms TTFT for shorter prompts and under 700ms for 8k sequences in streaming mode. Is that realistic?
[01:14] Samir: For hosted, yes we can get close, depends on batch sizes and whether you accept slightly lower tokenization coverage. For on-prem it's more about kernel selection + PCIe bandwidth on your cards.
[01:30] Anya: On-prem we have dual-socket machines with 4x H100s but using a standard PCIe bridge — we haven't tuned NVLink between them. Might be a factor for KV cache sharing.
[01:42] Priya: That matters a lot. KV cache transfers over PCIe are a common TTFT culprit, especially at first token when the system needs to materialize context. If you can enable NVLink or colocate on the same host, TTFT tends to drop significantly.
[01:55] Liam: We're largely on Colocation cages; we can request NVLink-enabled instances but it's a procurement ask.
[02:03] Maria: Quick Q: is TTFT dominated by model load or by first decode? In our tests the cold-start was the killer but once warmed it was okay.
[02:12] Priya: Two components — model load (if you're loading weights from disk or procssing from remote) and kernel kickoff / KV memcopy. Cold-starts where weights aren't resident are painful. For warm state, the kernel choice + compilation matters.
[02:30] Alex: Let's go through the benchmark table — I'll share screen — the key rows are: kernel tag, quantization (4-bit/8-bit/FP16), sequence length, streaming enabled, TTFT median, 95p, 99p, tokens/sec.
[02:45] [screen-sharing noises]
[03:10] Alex: For kernel A (fused-attn on FP16) at 2k seq we saw median TTFT 180ms, 95p 320ms. Kernel B (4-bit int8-like quant) had median 210ms, 95p 420ms but better steady-state throughput. The tail is worse under kernel B.
[03:30] Maria: Was the tail noise correlated to batching? Our traffic pattern is lots of small requests — 1-3 prompts — then occasional long 8k requests.
[03:40] Priya: Exactly. Small requests amplify scheduler jitter. Our recommendations: smaller batch window for low-latency routes, enable prefix-KV caching aggressively for repeated contexts, and on the long seqs use kernel A if you can accept higher memory.
[03:58] Thomas: What's the recommended batch window for sub-200ms TTFT?
[04:05] Samir: For sub-200ms median TTFT you want batching disabled for those routes or batching at <5ms, continuous streaming. But that lowers GPU utilization so cost goes up. It's a tradeoff.
[04:20] Liam: Cost vs latency is our main trade. We need to present numbers to product on how much more it costs to get the last 50ms.
[04:27] Alex: We'll provide the delta in the spreadsheet — cost per token with different batching windows.
[04:33] Maria: There was also something about chunking for streaming — rather than streaming every token you chunk N tokens then stream. Did you test chunk sizes?
[04:40] Priya: Yes. Chunking of 8-32 tokens reduces syscall overhead and can improve throughput and tail. But TTFT for the first chunk is still governed by kernel kickoff. For interactive UX, 8 token chunks feel smooth.
[04:55] Anya: In our web UX we need first visible token under 200ms ideally, but we can hide subsequent tokens with a spinner for a bit. So first chunk size 1 is preferred but not necessarily required.
[05:05] Alex: We'll mark that in recommendations: first chunk could be 1 token for perceived latency, then 8 token chunks thereafter.
[05:12] [06:00 minutes of side chatter about calendar invites omitted slightly]
[05:50] Maria: Any notes about compilation time? We saw a compile step that added ~120ms to cold starts. Is that avoidable?
[05:58] Priya: The compile step is JIT-style kernel specialization; you can precompile at deploy time with our artifact build so that cold-start compile isn't on the critical path. For private deploys we recommend pre-warming and shipping compiled kernels.
[06:12] Liam: Good — that's doable. We can request a build from Redwood with precompiled kernels.
[06:18] Alex: We'll include the build ids in the spreadsheet. Also note: quantization paths often require different kernels; if you're switching between quantized and FP16 at runtime you might get additional compile time.
[06:36] Thomas: If we commit to a single quantization profile for the POC, will that reduce variability?
[06:42] Samir: Yes, pick one profile per deploy to reduce compile jitter. We can help pick the best one for your accuracy targets.
[06:52] Maria: On accuracy, we saw a 1-2% rouge/bleu drop with aggressive 4-bit quant. That might be acceptable, but some of our fraud-detection internal models are sensitive.
[07:05] Priya: Important to run eval prompts — Redwood's Optimize suggestions include a quality-monitoring hook so we can trigger alerts if certain prompts degrade. We'll show that in the console.
[07:18] Liam: Can we get that hooked up to our internal alerting? PagerDuty?
[07:23] Alex: Yes — console supports webhooks; Priya can assist integrating.
[07:28] [08:00] Alex: Back to streaming: the hosted results show lower TTFT because we can allocate GPU right away and use faster PCIe NVLink configs. On-prem you'll vary.
[07:44] Anya: For our machines, we're about 90% sure NVLink is not enabled. I'll check with infra team. If we can't get NVLink, is there a kernel option that helps?
[07:55] Priya: There's an allocator optimization that reduces KV transfer by preferring local cache replicas; it's better for non-NVLink setups but increases memory usage a bit. We'll recommend that for rigs without NVLink. We'll note memory tradeoffs.
[08:12] Maria: For the on-prem benchmark you want streaming enabled with 8k sequences and also a mixed traffic pattern, right?
[08:19] Alex: Correct — please run 70% short prompts (<=512), 20% medium (512-2k), 10% long (2k-8k) with streaming on. Capture TTFT median/95/99 and tokens/sec, and note whether NVLink was enabled.
[08:34] Maria: Got it. We'll include sysinfo and pci configs.
[08:38] Liam: On batching: can Redwood route low-latency routes to a separate pool so we don't lose utilization on bulk jobs?
[08:45] Samir: Absolutely — routing policies are built in. You can pin low-latency routes to dedicated small pools and auto-fallback to higher-capacity pools in a burst scenario. That keeps cost predictable.
[08:58] Thomas: If we create a dedicated pool, is there a commit or reserved capacity pricing?
[09:04] Alex: For Dedicated we have reserved capacity options. We'll send pricing in the follow-up. For the POC we can get you short-term dedicated nodes.
[09:12] Maria: Another question: streaming on the client side — do you recommend websocket or server-sent events for browser UX?
[09:18] Priya: Websocket gives lower overhead and easier bidirectional, but SSE is simpler for one-way streaming. Both work. We have examples in the SDK.
[09:28] Anya: We use SSE at the moment.
[09:30] Priya: SSE should be fine, just tune chunk sizes.
[09:34] [10:00] Alex: Quick pause — any security blockers for running the on-prem perf runs?
[09:41] Liam: We'll need the SOC2 docs and network diagrams. Also confirm whether any logs leave the VPC — we need that for legal.
[09:50] Priya: For Private deploys nothing leaves unless you enable metrics forwarding. Redwood can run fully air-gapped if needed; otherwise we can ship the agent. I'll share SOC2 and a network diagram link after the call.
[09:59] Maria: Great. Also curious about audit logs — do you preserve raw prompts in the audit? We might need redaction.
[10:06] Priya: By default audit includes metadata and hashes, not raw prompt content. You can configure retention and masking. We'll include config snippets.
[10:15] Thomas: Good. If we move to a pilot in PROD we need SSO/SAML and RBAC integration. How long does that usually take?
[10:22] Alex: SSO is straightforward if you have IdP metadata ready — typically a day for initial setup, plus a week for testing in many cases. RBAC mapping depends on your role structure.
[10:31] Maria: Noted.
[10:33] [11:00] Alex: Back to kernels — Samir, can you summarize recommended kernel choices per seq length and quant level?
[10:36] Samir: Sure. Short: fused-attn FP16 (kernel A), gives best TTFT. Medium: fused-attn or optimized matmul with 8-bit quant if you need cost savings. Long (4k-8k): FP16 fused-attn or kernel tuned for KV mem efficiency; avoid aggressive 4-bit for long sequences because decoding accuracy suffers more. For non-NVLink hosts use the local-cache allocator. We'll add explicit build ids for each.
[10:58] Maria: Could you include latency deltas for switching between kernels? I want to show product the worst-case regression.
[11:03] Alex: Yes — spreadsheet will include delta columns and the raw logs.
[11:08] [12:00] Maria: About TTFT for streaming — can you clarify difference between TTFT and first-byte? I think some of our metrics are measuring renderer time rather than model start.
[11:15] Priya: TTFT is measured from request arrival at the load balancer to first token emitted by the model runtime. First-byte includes network and client render time. We'll give you instrumentation tips to measure both.
[11:28] Liam: We'll instrument both and share.
[11:32] Alex: Ok, quick risk register: compile jitter, NVLink absence, binpacking leading to noisy neighbors, and quantization accuracy. Any other risks?
[11:42] Thomas: Procurement delay for NVLink-enabled machines could push timelines. Also internal security review for network egress.
[11:49] Priya: We'll prepare mitigation notes: precompile artifacts, local cache allocator, dedicated small pools for low-latency traffic, and docs for egress control.
[11:58] Maria: For the on-prem run we'll try to reproduce the hosted GPU topology as best as we can. If results are much worse we'll set up a run on Redwood dedicated so you can compare directly.
[12:08] Alex: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[12:12] Maria: None from me.
[12:14] Liam: All good.
[12:16] Alex: Recap of next steps: Alex send kernel spreadsheet + build ids; Priya send SOC2 & network diag; Maria run on-prem 8k seq test and upload results; Samir/Alex schedule a deeper streaming deep-dive if on-prem numbers lag. We'll aim to reconvene next week same time.
[12:35] Thomas: Thanks everyone.
[12:37] Alex: Thanks — meeting adjourned.

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcription had a few mislabels (kernel vs colon) and occasional ASR errors on acronyms like NVLink and KV cache (appears as K V catche).
